title: The ungrateful guest
hookLine: He gave you life, food and body, and you forget Him (Sukhmani 4)

lines: A GUEST WHO STAYS A WEEK.
NO THANK-YOU, NOT EVEN A NAME.
THE GUEST IS ANY ONE OF US.
cards: A guest stays a week. The hosts give up their best room. They cook every meal, wash the towels, drive the guest to the airport at dawn.
And the guest leaves without saying thank you, without even remembering the hosts' names by the time the plane lands. Sukhmani never uses the word guest in these stanzas.
But the fourth ashtpadi tells a story very like it, and the guest is the human being, any one of us, fed and housed and carried, and forgetting the host.

teach.h: THE WOMB, THE MILK, THE YOUTH, OLD AGE.
teach.b: The first stanza walks through a whole life, in paraphrase. Think of the virtues of the all-pervading One, O mortal: from what beginnings were you made?
The One who formed you, shaped you and adorned you, who kept you safe in the fire of the womb. In infancy, gave you milk to drink. In the fullness of youth, food, comfort and understanding.
And in old age, family and friends gather round to feed you as you sit.
Then the turn: this one without virtue doesn't appreciate a single good thing done for them; only if You forgive, says Nanak, are they accepted. The next stanza lists what an ordinary day is made of.
By whose grace you live at ease on the earth, laughing with children, siblings, friends and spouse.
By whose grace you drink cool water, and have the gentle breeze and priceless fire. By whose grace you enjoy every pleasure. Who gave you hands and feet, ears, eyes and a tongue.
And you forsake that One, and attach yourself to others. Notice what's on the list. Not miracles.
Laughter with family. Hands. Things so ordinary they're noticed only when they're gone.
Ingratitude, here, isn't usually cruelty. It's forgetfulness: the guest who never noticed who made the bed. And the cure is just as ordinary.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the fourth ashtpadi, and Sikh practice turns their lesson into habit through shukrana, giving thanks to Waheguru, in daily prayer and the Ardas.

o: a wise elder whose words are a gift
the giver, the One who gives everything
a servant who brings food to the table

games.q: what was given — tap the pairs.

s: the stanzas use the word guest
the image of the guest is ours; the text walks through a life of gifts.
the stanza lists ordinary gifts like cool water and a breeze
water, breeze, fire, hands, ears, eyes and tongue.
the stanzas say acceptance comes only by the One's forgiveness
only if You forgive, says Nanak, are they accepted.

games.q: you've been given milk, water, breath, hands, family. according to the fourth ashtpadi, what does the human usually do?
o: forget the giver and attach to other things.
try to pay the giver back.
games.why: the stanza says the one without virtue doesn't appreciate a single good thing, and forsakes the giver for others.

practice: Pick three ordinary gifts from the stanza that you have right now: water you drank today, hands that work, someone who made you laugh this week.
For each one, breathe in and notice it as if for the first time, and breathe out with thanks, adding Waheguru if you pray, to the One the stanza calls the giver.

wordCard.voice: Daataa, the giver: Sukhmani's fourth ashtpadi says the One gave you the womb's shelter, milk, youth, water, breeze and hands, and the human forgets the giver.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daataa, the giver; a common Gurbani name for God.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the giver. Even the water had someone pouring it. Day four hundred fifty-one, done.

sources.ref: Gauri Sukhmani M5, ashtpadi 4, pauris 1–2, Ang 266
